title: Find a missing side length from the area

lesson.title: Working Backwards to Find a Missing Side

steps.say: You already know that the area of a rectangle is the length times the width. Today we do that same thing backwards: we know the area and one side, and we go hunting for the side that is missing.

visual.caption: Five times three gives fifteen square centimetres.

steps.say: Here is the trick. Since area is made by multiplying, we get a side back by dividing. Imagine a flower bed at a Burnaby community garden. It covers forty-eight square metres, and one side measures eight metres. Ask yourself: eight times what number makes forty-eight? Division answers that question for us.

visual.caption: Forty-eight square metres, with eight in every row.

steps.say: So we divide. Forty-eight divided by eight is six, so the missing side is six metres. Now let us be good detectives and check it: six times eight is forty-eight square metres. It matches, so we know we are right.

visual.caption: Eight metres by six metres — area forty-eight square metres.

steps.say: Watch out for one sneaky mistake. Some people subtract and say forty-eight take away eight is forty, so the side must be forty metres. Let us test that. Eight times forty is three hundred twenty square metres — that is a giant field, way bigger than our flower bed! Subtracting cannot undo multiplying. Only dividing can.

visual.caption: Eight by forty would be three hundred twenty square metres — much too big.

steps.say: So whenever a side is missing, take the area, divide by the side you know, and then multiply your answer back to make sure it fits.

lesson.answer: Area divided by the side you know gives the side you are missing — then multiply back to check.

practice.question: A rectangular vegetable patch in a Victoria backyard has an area of sixty-three square metres. One side of it is nine metres long. How long is the other side? Draw the rectangle yourself and label the side you know.
practice.answer: Seven metres, because sixty-three divided by nine is seven — and checking, nine times seven is sixty-three square metres.
